title: Multireference perturbation theory with nonorthogonal determinants
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce NOCI-RSPT, a framework for constructing perturb-then-diagonalize multireference perturbation theories for model spaces defined by nonorthogonal determinants. NOCI-RSPT realizes order-by-order size consistency by orthogonalizing the effective Hamiltonian before perturbatively truncating it and removes problematic internal excitations through model-space projection. The resulting second- and third-order theories, NOCI-RS2 and NOCI-RS3, recover MP2 and MP3 in the single-reference limit and exhibit the same respective cost scaling at fixed model-space size. Calculations on assemblies of multireference $\mathrm{H}_2$ fragments demonstrate size consistency, while calculations of the low-energy states of $\mathrm{H}_2$ along its dissociation curve demonstrate improved numerical stability and characterize the influence of intruder states. The latter calculations demonstrate the exceptional accuracy achieved by NOCI-RS3 and illustrate how model-space expansion and amplitude regularization can mitigate the effects of large perturbative corrections. Altogether, NOCI-RSPT provides a systematic route to low-scaling multireference perturbation theories built from single-reference methods.

title: OPRD-Imp: a dataset of experimentally observed impurities and side products in multi-step pharmaceutical syntheses
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07488v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predicting reaction impurities is a critical yet persistently data-limited challenge in pharmaceutical process chemistry. While machine learning models for reaction outcome prediction have advanced rapidly, benchmarking their ability to predict impurities remains impractical due to the absence of curated, publicly accessible datasets. We present OPRD-Imp, a dataset of 229 organic reactions drawn from 62 publications in Organic Process Research & Development, each annotated with experimentally observed impurities and their mechanistic origins. A total of 784 impurity entries is provided, classified into four origin categories. Reactions are represented as reaction SMILES and impurities as individual SMILES strings, with multi-step synthetic route connectivity preserved. All data were manually extracted from the source publications by trained chemists following a standardized extraction protocol, with expert chemical validation and manual structure drawing. OPRD-Imp is intended to serve as a benchmark resource for evaluating models that predict reaction impurities, providing experimentally reported impurity annotations and mechanistic origin labels that are not systematically represented in conventional reaction datasets.

title: Heat Transport Mechanisms in MOF-5
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We find that MOF-5 supports both long-lived phonons and linker vibrations whose split spectra signal a breakdown of the phonon quasiparticle approximation. Combining mode-projected molecular dynamics spectra with spectral Wigner heat transport, we resolve two contrasting transport channels: low-frequency particle-like phonon propagation decreases strongly from 200 to 500 K, whereas wave-like phonon coherence remains nearly constant and supplies about half the intrinsic conductivity at 500 K. A phenomenological extrinsic scattering model provides a plausible explanation for the discrepancy between calculated and measured conductivities in terms of both its magnitude and temperature dependence. We also identify signatures of phonon quasiparticle breakdown in the linker vibrations of ZIF-8 and HKUST-1, indicating that this feature extends to other metal-organic frameworks.

title: Updated Tkatchenko Scheffler method and assessment of dispersion methods for alkali-containing systems
abstract:
arXiv:2608.01501v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The Tkatchenko-Scheffler (TS) pairwise method to calculate dispersion interactions is a widely used approach to incorporate missing long-range van der Waals contributions in semilocal and hybrid density functional calculations. Despite subsequent many-body extensions, this formulation remains widely used. In 2018, Fedorov et al. reported updated van der Waals radii to the seminal work published in 2009. The present work examines the accuracy of the TS method with updated van der Waals radii (TS_2018), coupled with the semilocal Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof density functional, for structural predictions of semiconducting and insulating materials. Special attention is paid to materials containing alkali elements, for which the TS_2009 method exhibits a large overbinding, associated with potentially large errors in predicted atomic structures. We also consider a narrower reformulation (TS_alkali) where only the the alkali atoms are corrected, so the method remains otherwise compatible with TS_2009. We compare these methods with a broader set of dispersion corrections--the DFT-D3 method, the exchange-hole dipole moment method, and the beyond-pairwise, nonlocal many-body dispersion method--for ionic and alkali-containing systems more generally. We examine equilibrium geometry predictions for 45 inorganic solid compounds as well as three Cs-containing halide perovskites, CsPb$X_3$ ($X$ = Cl, Br, I). Our results show that the updated van der Waals radii in the TS_2018 and TS_alkali methods resolve the overbinding that is present with TS_2009 in alkali-containing systems, bringing predictions into closer agreement with other dispersion methods. For the halide perovskites, method-dependent differences in predicted cell volumes and shapes persist, and no approach performs with perfect accuracy on all metrics for all three materials.

title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08438v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.

title: Ab initio simulation of excited-state potential energy surfaces with transferable deep quantum Monte Carlo
abstract:
Nature Computational Science, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s43588-026-01065-y
Transferable deep-learning quantum Monte Carlo for molecular excited states is introduced. Sharing parameters, an ansatz represents the wavefunction across molecular geometries and states, reducing the cost of modeling potential energy surfaces.

title: Interaction embedding via factorized linear models for multi-element machine learning interatomic potentials
abstract: Linear machine-learning interatomic potentials, such as the Ultra-Fast Force Field (UF3), deliver near-density functional theory accuracy at low computational cost. Their number of parameters, however, grows combinatorially with the number of chemical species, limiting their use on multi-element systems. We address this scaling problem with pseudo-interaction UF3 (PI-UF3), a factorized linear model in which the Z(k) real k-body potentials are expressed as linear combinations of a small number P(k) ≪ Z(k) of shared pseudo-interactions. Learned element embeddings are standard in nonlinear potentials; inside a linear model, the embedding becomes a rank constraint on the coefficient matrix of each body order, and the resulting bilinear problem is trained with alternating least squares, where each block update is one closed-form linear solve. We benchmark PI-UF3 on a five-element refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) and a subset of MD22, training on forces, with restarts and cross-validation. On the chemically homogeneous HEA, compression acts as implicit regularization: with three-body terms included, PI-UF3’s test force root-mean-squared error drops below the unfactorized UF3 baseline with 3% of the baseline’s parameters on the predefined split and 7% on every cross-validation fold, and the maximally compressed model recovers a chemically meaningful ordering of homonuclear interaction strengths consistent with experimental bulk melting temperatures. On the chemically heterogeneous MD22 subset, where UF3 is not expressive enough to overfit, PI-UF3 approaches the baseline from above and reaches parity with it at about two thirds of the parameter count. Compression thus regularizes only where the unfactorized model overfits, while a parameter reduction is available in both regimes.
relevance_reason: Develops and benchmarks a factorized linear machine-learned interatomic potential on alloys and MD22, clearly satisfying (a)-(c).

title: Ab initio -based intermolecular potential for normal hydrogen, orthohydrogen, and parahydrogen: Prediction of thermodynamic behavior
abstract: An ab initio-based intermolecular potential is reported for normal hydrogen, orthohydrogen, and parahydrogen. Molecular simulations for thermodynamic properties and calculations of the second virial coefficients demonstrate very good agreement with reference values for both the nuclear spin isomers of hydrogen. The thermodynamic behavior studied includes vapor–liquid equilibria, energy, enthalpy, heat capacities, isochoric pressure coefficient, isobaric thermal expansion coefficient, isothermal compressibility, Joule–Thomson coefficient, and speed of sound. The simulations extend from low (cryogenic) to ambient temperatures and pressures of up to 100 MPa. Quantum effects have an important influence on the behavior of these properties, which, in some cases, are not limited to the intermolecular potential contribution to the energy. That is, the enthalpy, heat capacities, Joule–Thomson coefficient, and speed of sound are also significantly affected by quantum effects on the kinetic energy. The simulation values may be more reliable than existing reference data in some instances. This is particularly the case for the thermodynamic properties of orthohydrogen that cannot be measured directly.
relevance_reason: Develops an ab initio-based intermolecular potential for hydrogen spin isomers and runs molecular simulations of thermodynamic properties, satisfying (a)-(c).

title: Global coarse-grained simulation of hierarchical self-assembly in AB n  dendron-like giant molecules: Phase behavior, molecular packing, and the role of rigidity
abstract: We present a global dissipative particle dynamics simulation study of hierarchical self-assembly in ABn dendron-like giant molecules, drawing upon the experimental platform where hydrophilic and hydrophobic polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane cages serve as the amphiphilic building blocks. Without imposing any pre-assumed structural bias, our coarse-grained model spontaneously evolves from disordered melts into lamellar, double gyroid, hexagonal cylinder, and spherical micelle phases as the number of hydrophobic peripheral units increases—a sequence that faithfully mirrors experimental observations. A key innovation lies in comparing three topologically isomeric representations of the molecular building block: a rigid cage, a flexible chain, and a ring. This systematic comparison reveals that molecular rigidity alone can significantly alter phase boundaries and reduce micelle sizes, a finding that disentangles the role of shape persistence from that of composition or molecular weight. Our simulations further uncover hidden organizational features, including ordered linker arrays within lamellar interphases and the emergence of perforated lamellar structures upon linker elongation. While complete ordering into Frank–Kasper lattices remains computationally demanding, statistical characterizations of the spherical micelles consistently recover experimental trends, affirming the predictive capacity of our approach. This work establishes global coarse-grained simulation as an effective tool for exploring the rich phase behavior of giant molecules and lays the groundwork for the modular, in silico design of programmable supramolecular materials.
relevance_reason: Coarse-grained dissipative particle dynamics simulations of dendron-like giant molecules self-assembly, satisfying (a)-(c) via coarse-grained MD.

title: Effect of added salts on the interfacial dynamics of monovalent metal ions and model water-soluble polymers
abstract: Traditional theories of electrolyte and polyelectrolyte solutions overlook ion and polymer hydration, yielding an overly idealized perspective of the thermodynamic and dynamic properties of these solutions. In particular, the propensity of certain ions to increase or decrease the water diffusion coefficient at low solution concentrations is poorly understood, a phenomenon that correlates strongly with the Hofmeister series, which describes the influence of salts on the solubility and self-assembly of synthetic and biological macromolecules, as well as colloidal particles. These ion-specific effects have profound ramifications in diverse biological, medical science, and technological applications. We address the general problem of understanding ion and uncharged water-soluble polymer hydration through molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of representative water-soluble polymers, polyacrylamide and polyethylene oxide, in aqueous salt solutions. Careful attention is given to the capacity of our model to reproduce observed trends of added monovalent salts on the diffusion coefficient of water. Reproducing these ion-specific trends in the mobility of water has been a recurrent challenge in prior MD simulations of aqueous solutions based on a physically realistic model of water. Our work on salt solutions represents an important advance on which we build our modeling of aqueous polymer solutions with added salts. Simulations of our model polymers reveal an extended nanoscale dynamic hydration layer having a scale on the order of 1 nm, in which the mobility is perturbed from its bulk value, and the mobility gradient in this layer appears to obey a near universal functional form.
relevance_reason: Classical MD simulations of polymers and monovalent ions in aqueous salt solutions, satisfying (a)-(c).

title: Estimating Irving-Kirkwood pressure profiles from per-atom virial and density profiles: a closure for the contour-dependent term in planar liquid films
abstract:
arXiv:2610.41906v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The local pressure tensor of an inhomogeneous fluid is not unique. Two tangential profiles are in common use in planar simulations: the Irving-Kirkwood (IK) profile, which requires a dedicated pass over every pair of atoms for every slab, and the per-atom virial (PAV) profile, which molecular-dynamics codes produce at negligible cost and coincides with the Harasima contour. The two differ by the derivative of a pair quantity, P_T^IK - P_T^PAV = dQ/dz. We show that, for Lennard-Jones free-standing films, Q(z) can be predicted from the density profile and the bulk radial distribution function of the coexisting liquid: under the closure rho2(r1,r2) ~ rho(z1) rho(z2) g(r12), with a pair-local interpolation of g between its liquid and dilute limits, Q is a double integral of rho(z) against a kernel built from u'(r) g(r). The estimator P_T^IK,est = P_T^PAV + dQ/dz is tested against IK profiles measured on the same trajectories for 20 films (thicknesses 7-25 sigma, three cutoff radii, two temperatures): the root-mean-square residual is 0.001-0.002 epsilon/sigma^3, against 0.010-0.021 for the uncorrected profile, and Q, the amount that the contour choice transfers between the two interfaces of a film with non-equivalent surfaces, is recovered to within 0.6% of the surface tension. Applied to the normal component, the same closure removes 83-92% of the spurious structure of the per-atom zz profile, a test that needs no IK run. Its mixture form is validated on three two-component films with an adsorbate unequally distributed between their faces, where it resolves the tension of each face; a clean face recovers the tension of the pure film.
relevance_reason: Classical Lennard-Jones molecular dynamics of free-standing liquid films used to derive a closure for the contour-dependent Irving-Kirkwood pressure-tensor term; explicit atoms (a), classical MD force fields (b) and clear method development (c) with validation on 20 simulated films.

title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07723v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.
relevance_reason: The paper introduces an all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework (BILBY-MD) with motif-drift and free-energy landscape analysis for protein motif scaffolding designs; explicit atoms (a), MD/free-energy methodology (b), and application to assess designed protein systems (c) are all satisfied.

title: Automatic generation of exchange–correlation response kernels
abstract: Computing density-functional response properties requires contracting derivatives of the exchange–correlation (xc) energy with perturbed densities on a grid. While the xc functional’s derivatives have long been available to high orders from libraries such as Libxc, the surrounding contraction layer—the chain rule that combines them with the grid-based basis-function and density data into the total xc contribution—has instead been hand-derived and hand-coded in every program, for every functional family, spin case, and property. We present libxckernel, a library that automatically generates this layer by symbolic differentiation. The xc functional’s ingredients are expressed as sesquilinear forms in the density matrix, so the xc energy can be differentiated to any order while the functional derivatives remain opaque. The basis functions and the orbital coefficients may both be complex. The chain rule then produces any xc matrix element: Fock matrices, orbital Hessians, or any other response terms of any order. Terms sharing a pattern are collapsed for efficiency. Extensible plugins emit the expressions as NumPy Einstein sums, compiled C++ kernels with C/Fortran interfaces, or host-program specific source code. libxckernel is free and open-source software under the BSD-3-Clause license, enabling rapid implementation of functionality missing from many electronic structure programs. We demonstrate it by extending Psi4 with meta-generalized gradient approximation (mGGA) response kernels for orbital stability analysis and time-dependent density-functional theory (TD-DFT), GGA and mGGA analytic nuclear Hessians, and exact quadrature grid response, as well as by extending GPAW with mGGA and triplet TD-DFT kernels and gradient-corrected kernels for periodic dielectric response.
relevance_reason: DFT exchange-correlation response-kernel generation via symbolic differentiation advances electronic-structure methodology, satisfying (b)-(c) as DFT method development, though it is infrastructure rather than a direct dynamics simulation.
